newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dalgety warns on profits, shares dive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dalgety warns on profits, shares dive.

text.p: British petfoods and agricultural feeds firm Dalgety Plc said on Tuesday full-year profits would be lower than expected because of poor fourth-quarter trading and higher exceptional charges.

The group warned exceptional charges, earlier forecast at 36 million pounds ($60.6 million), were now expected to total 138 million and it now expected pre-tax profit for the year of not less than 65 million pounds.
The statement, which included a more than doubling of an exceptional charge to reorganise its petfood division, sent the group's shares plummeting 40 pence to 220 pence in early trade.
In the year to June 30, 1996 Dalgety reported pre-tax profits excluding exceptional items of 101.9 million pounds down from 127.1 million.
The group suffered from a very poor fourth quarter's trading in agriculture with the arable supply business hit by low priced fertiliser imports and the wettest June on record in Britain.

Dalgety, which reiterated its earlier forecast to pay a final dividend of at least six pence per share, also said exceptional costs for its petfoods division had now more than doubled to 67 million pounds.

"There will be a lot more scepticism this time round as to the benefits of restructuring. There were a lot of shocked faces around today. It has just come so soon after their last one. It did surprise a lot of people and the size of the extra exceptional is quite stunning," said one analyst, who declined to be named.

Other analysts shared his scepticism about the group's recovery plan, saying the market for animal feed has changed irreparably since the BSE crisis and the dumping of cheaper feed from Eastern Europe.
"Farmers just do not trust big feed manufacturers anymore, although I can see how they might turnaround the petfoods business," said one analyst.

The EU banned British beef sales world-wide after Britain acknowledged there could be a link between Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) and Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, the human equivalent of the brain-wasting illness.
Many farmers blame food manufacturers for providing them with poor quality animal feed.
But the group's management is determined to turn the business around, said its chief executive Richard Clothier in an interview.
"I believe that as a result of this announcement we can look forward to a substantial improvement this year and next," said Clothier.
"I am very encouraged by the tough thinking and hard line taken by our finance director."

Kenneth Hanna took over from John Martyn as finance director on May 1. Hanna has taken a more prudent approach to accounting for bad debt provisions, insurance claims and the value put on assets, Clothier said.
"We have got to turn around the petfoods business. We have got to concentrate on fixing it. We have not got our costs down fast enough."

Hugh Donaldson, who took over from Nigel Garrow as chief executive of Petfoods two months ago, has identified more areas where costs can be saved, Clothier said. This will involve job losses and plant closures but Clothier said he could not yet give details.

Changes at the group's petfoods division will produce savings of some 20 million pounds per annum, with 8.0 million coming through in 1997/98 and 12 million the year after, said Clothier. In May the group calculated a shake-up in its petfoods division would bring a benefit of 12 million stg. Dalgety's main petfood brands include Felix, Winalot, Prime and Bonus.

As well as an increase in charges for its petfoods business, the group made additional provisions for surplus property of 15 million and an accounting adjustment for goodwill of up to 50 million to be made in the 1997 accounts.

On trading, Clothier said a dry spring period meant cattle grazed for longer and reduced the need for animal feed. June, which is an important month for fertiliser sales by Dalgety, was exceptionally wet which prevented farmers from getting into fields to fertilise or to spray pesticide onto their crops. ($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
